Can you tell me about the Franconia Ridge Loop? I've heard it's one of the best hikes in New Hampshire.

The Franconia Ridge Loop is widely considered one of the finest hikes in the Northeast — and for good reason. It strings together three 4,000-foot summits (Little Haystack, Mt. Lincoln, and Mt. Lafayette) along a narrow, exposed ridge with panoramic views in every direction. Here's what you need to know:

**The basics**
- Distance: 8.9 miles round trip (loop)
- Elevation gain: ~3,900 ft
- Typical time: 6–9 hours depending on pace
- Region: Franconia Notch, off I-93

**What the hike is like**
You'll climb via the Falling Waters Trail past a series of waterfalls to Little Haystack, then walk the open ridge north to Lincoln and Lafayette. The ridge section — about 1.7 miles fully above treeline — is the highlight of the hike and its main commitment. You descend via the Bridle Path through Greenleaf Hut back to the trailhead.

**Two hazards to know about**
These are distinct and worth understanding separately:

*Weather exposure:* The ridge is fully open to wind from both sides with no shelter for the entire traverse. Afternoon thunderstorms are the most serious risk in summer — this is one of the most lightning-exposed ridges in the White Mountains. Check the [Mt. Washington Observatory Higher Summits Forecast](https://www.mountwashington.org/experience-the-weather/higher-summits-forecast/) before you go, start early enough to complete the ridge before early afternoon if any storms are possible, and carry a full rain layer and insulation even on sunny days.

*Fall risk:* The ridge trail itself is straightforward with minimal drop-off exposure. The Falling Waters descent is steeper, with rocky switchbacks and a narrow section near Cloudland Falls where the trail edge has a drop into the ravine. Trekking poles are strongly recommended for the descent, and the wet rocks around the waterfalls deserve extra care.

**Is it right for you?**
It's a big day — nearly 3,900 ft of gain is real work — but it's not technically difficult. If you're comfortable on full-day hikes and have solid footwear, it's very achievable. If you're newer to the Whites, consider building up with a shorter hike like Welch-Dickey first to get a feel for above-treeline terrain at lower stakes.

**Useful links**
- [USFS WMNF — Franconia Notch Trails](https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/whitemountain/recreation/recarea/?recid=74900) — check for current closures
- [AllTrails — Franconia Ridge Loop](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/franconia-ridge-loop-trail) — recent trip reports and conditions
- [Greenleaf Hut](https://www.outdoors.org/destinations/new-hampshire/greenleaf-hut/) — AMC hut on the route, useful weather bailout point

What time of year are you thinking of going?

I want to hike Mt. Washington someday but I've never really done anything serious in the mountains. Where do I even start? I'm reasonably fit from running but have zero hiking experience.

Great goal — and your running fitness is a real asset, though hiking uses your legs differently enough that building up gradually still matters. Here's a realistic progression that gets you to Washington prepared rather than just lucky.

**What you're building toward**
Mt. Washington via Lion's Head is 8 miles with 3,825 ft of gain. The fitness is manageable for a runner; what takes preparation is the above-treeline commitment — 2.8 miles of fully exposed terrain where weather can turn dangerous fast. The progression below builds both your legs and your judgment.

---

**Step 1 — Welch-Dickey Loop** *(4.4 miles, 1,750 ft)*
Start here. It introduces open granite slab terrain and a short above-treeline section at forgiving scale. The slabs are the point — they teach you to read terrain and trust your footwear. Main hazard: fall risk on the slabs when wet. Check the forecast for rain timing before you go.
[AllTrails — Welch-Dickey](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/welch-dickey-loop-trail)

**Step 2 — Mt. Moosilauke via Beaver Brook** *(7.8 miles, 3,020 ft)*
Your first real 4,000-footer and your first fully committed above-treeline summit. The broad open plateau is genuinely exposed to weather and disorienting in fog — this is where you start building weather awareness as a habit. Note: the Beaver Brook Trail runs alongside waterfalls with real drop-off fall risk on the trail edges; stay on the marked path.
[AllTrails — Moosilauke via Beaver Brook](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/beaver-brook-trail-to-mount-moosilauke)

**Step 3 — Franconia Ridge Loop** *(8.9 miles, 3,900 ft)*
This is the key step before Washington. 1.7 miles of above-treeline ridge walking, three 4K summits, and your first experience managing weather decisions on an exposed traverse. Complete this hike comfortably — meaning you checked the forecast, set a turnaround time, and the day went to plan — before moving to Washington.
[AllTrails — Franconia Ridge Loop](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/franconia-ridge-loop-trail)

**Step 4 — Mt. Washington via Lion's Head** *(8.0 miles, 3,825 ft)*
Now you're ready. The fitness and terrain are similar to what you've done; the difference is Washington's weather severity. Always check the [Mt. Washington Observatory Higher Summits Forecast](https://www.mountwashington.org/experience-the-weather/higher-summits-forecast/) — not the valley forecast — the morning of your hike. Set a turnaround time before you leave the trailhead and honor it.
[USFS — Mt. Washington Trails](https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/whitemountain/recreation/recarea/?recid=74930)

---

**A note on timing**
If you're starting from zero, this progression is realistic across one hiking season. Do Welch-Dickey early, Moosilauke mid-season, Franconia Ridge when you feel solid, and Washington late summer when conditions are most stable. Don't rush the steps — each one is genuinely fun, not just training.

What season are you planning to start, and are you thinking of doing these solo or with others?

Planning to do Mt Washington via Lion's Head in late September. I've done a bunch of 4K footers this summer. What gear do I actually need — not the ultralight minimalist take, but what's genuinely appropriate for late September?

Late September on Washington is shoulder season in practice even if it's technically still fall — ice on the upper trail is possible from mid-October but a cold front can push that earlier. Here's what's genuinely appropriate, split by what it addresses.

**For weather exposure** (the dominant hazard above treeline)
- **Hardshell jacket and pants** — not a soft shell, not a rain poncho. Wind on the summit regularly exceeds 60 mph and a hardshell is the only thing that works. Arc'teryx Alpha-tier or equivalent; this is not a place to cheap out.
- **Insulating layer** — a midweight fleece or synthetic puffy that fits under your hardshell. September summit temps average in the 30s–40s°F but wind chill can push that well below freezing.
- **Hat, balaclava, gloves** — the balaclava is optional if conditions look mild but it weighs nothing and September can surprise you.
- **Emergency bivy or space blanket** — add this in shoulder season. If you get caught in deteriorating weather it buys time.

**For fall risk** (secondary but real on the rocky upper trail)
- **Waterproof hiking boots with ankle support** — the rocky steps below Lion's Head and the boulder field above treeline are uneven and demanding on ankles. Trail runners are marginal here in wet conditions.
- **Trekking poles** — especially for the descent. The rocky trail is hard on knees and poles reduce slip risk significantly.
- **Microspikes in your pack** — by late September there's a real chance of ice on the upper trail after a cold night. They weigh almost nothing and the alternative is turning around.

**Navigation and planning**
- Carry the [AMC Presidential Range map](https://www.outdoors.org/resources/amc-outdoors/gear-and-skills/trail-maps/presidential-range-map/) — no cell service above treeline.
- Check the [Mt. Washington Observatory Higher Summits Forecast](https://www.mountwashington.org/experience-the-weather/higher-summits-forecast/) the morning of your hike, not the night before. Conditions change overnight.
- Set a turnaround time before you leave Pinkham Notch and write it down. Most incidents on Washington involve hikers who didn't honor theirs.

**What you probably don't need for a late September day hike**
Crampons and ice axe — unless the forecast shows overnight temperatures well below freezing and confirmed ice on the upper trail. Check AllTrails trip reports from the week before for current upper trail conditions.

My family is visiting the White Mountains in mid-October, first time for all of us. Two adults and a 10-year-old. We hike occasionally but nothing serious. What would you recommend?

Mid-October is a beautiful time in the Whites — foliage is at or just past peak at elevation, the crowds have thinned, and the air is crisp. With a 10-year-old and occasional hiking experience, here are three options that match your group well.

**Best pick: Lonesome Lake Loop** *(3.2 miles, 1,000 ft)*
This is the standout family hike for your situation. The trail climbs through forest to a quiet mountain lake with direct views of the Franconia Ridge. It's genuinely beautiful, manageable for a 10-year-old, and Lonesome Lake Hut at the top is a great turnaround point (check if it's still staffed in mid-October). Mostly below treeline so no weather exposure concerns. Allow 3–4 hours.
[AllTrails — Lonesome Lake](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/lonesome-lake-trail)

**Good alternative: Welch-Dickey Loop** *(4.4 miles, 1,750 ft)*
A step up in length and challenge but rewards the effort with open granite slab views that feel genuinely alpine. The slabs are the highlight — and the one thing to know: they're slippery when wet, so check the rain forecast before you go. In dry October conditions this is excellent for a capable 10-year-old who likes climbing on rocks. Allow 4–5 hours.
[AllTrails — Welch-Dickey](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/welch-dickey-loop-trail)

**If your group wants something shorter: Mt. Tecumseh** *(5.0 miles, 2,200 ft)*
Slightly longer than Lonesome Lake but well-graded and entirely forested — great foliage views in the trees. No technical terrain. A solid first 4K footer if the group is feeling ambitious.
[AllTrails — Mt. Tecumseh](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/new-hampshire/mount-tecumseh-trail)

**October-specific note**
Mid-October in the Whites means temperatures in the 30s–40s°F at trailhead, colder with wind at elevation. Bring more layers than you think you need — a fleece and a windproof outer layer for everyone, including the 10-year-old. Microspikes aren't usually needed this early in October but it's worth checking recent trip reports the week before for any early ice reports.

Which of these sounds most appealing for your group? I can give you more detail on any of them.

Heading up Lion's Head this Saturday. Observatory is showing 45mph winds at the summit with temps around 38F, partly cloudy. Is that workable?

45 mph sustained with 38°F is manageable but not comfortable — wind chill puts you around 20°F. A few things to factor in:

**What makes it workable**
- Partly cloudy means visibility should be reasonable — navigation isn't a concern
- 38°F base temp means hypothermia risk is real but not acute if you're dressed properly
- 45 mph sustained is strong but well within normal Washington conditions; the trail below the cone is sheltered enough that you won't feel the full brunt until the upper alpine zone

**What to watch**
- Check the forecast again Saturday morning — Observatory updates overnight and a gust forecast above 60 mph changes the calculus
- The ridge traverse between Lion's Head and the summit cone is the most exposed section; that's where 45 mph will feel like 45 mph
- Make sure your hardshell is genuinely wind-rated, not just water-resistant — at those speeds a soft shell is inadequate

**Gear for these specific conditions**
Full hardshell (jacket and pants), insulating mid-layer, balaclava, liner gloves plus shell gloves, and goggles if you have them — 45 mph blows grit and ice crystals. Trekking poles will help on the descent.

If the gust forecast Saturday morning is showing 60+ mph or the partly cloudy has shifted to overcast with precipitation, I'd reconsider. At 45 mph and clear skies, it's a good day with the right kit.

Check the [Higher Summits Forecast](https://www.mountwashington.org/experience-the-weather/higher-summits-forecast/) Saturday morning before leaving Pinkham.

I've done Washington, Lafayette, Lincoln, and Moosilauke so far. I want to knock out as many of the Presidentials as I can next season. What's the most efficient approach?

Good base to work from — you've already done the two hardest Presidentials (Washington and the northern peaks are comparable in commitment). Here's how to work through the rest efficiently.

**The southern Presidentials — easiest cluster to stack**
Pierce, Eisenhower, Monroe, and Franklin can all be combined in logical pairings from the Crawford Notch side. 

- **Pierce + Eisenhower** via Crawford Path from Crawford Depot is a natural pairing — 9.5 miles round trip, 2,900 ft. Well-graded, good above-treeline terrain on Eisenhower's dome. A strong choice for an early season warmup.
- **Monroe + Washington** — you've done Washington, so adding Monroe (which sits just below Lakes of the Clouds Hut on the Ammonoosuc Ravine route) on a second Washington day via a different approach is efficient. The Ammonoosuc Ravine Trail is steeper but shorter than Lion's Head.
- **Franklin** is usually tagged from Monroe since it's a short side trip on the Crawford Path ridge.

**The northern Presidentials — commit to a full day**
Adams, Jefferson, and Madison are best done as a ridge traverse rather than separate out-and-backs. The classic approach is the Air Line Trail to Adams, then south to Jefferson via Gulfside Trail, back via the Caps Ridge Trail to the Valley Way trailhead — a long 12-13 mile day but the most efficient way to collect three peaks. This requires a car shuttle or a willing driver. Weather exposure is severe for the entire traverse — these peaks are at least as committing as Washington.

**Wildcat A and Carter Dome** round out the Presidentials area and are best paired together from the Carter Notch side.

**Order suggestion for the season**
1. Pierce + Eisenhower (early season, moderate day, good for shaking off winter)
2. Adams + Jefferson + Madison traverse (pick your best weather window — this is your biggest day)
3. Monroe via Ammonoosuc (combine with another Washington attempt or stand-alone)
4. Wildcat A + Carter Dome

How many trips are you planning, and are you working with a partner or solo? That changes the logistics on the northern traverse.
